Paged Attention, a technique popularized by the vLLM framework, fundamentally rethinks how Key-Value (KV) caches are managed during autoregressive decoding by borrowing concepts from operating system memory management. Instead of allocating contiguous memory blocks for each sequence, which leads to significant waste due to variable sequence lengths, Paged Attention divides the KV cache into fixed-size physical blocks. These blocks are managed through a logical abstraction known as the **block table**.

During the decoding process, each request is assigned a block table, which acts as a mapping between logical block indices (representing the sequence position) and physical block indices (representing actual GPU memory locations). When a new token is generated, the system checks if the current physical block is full. If it is, a new physical block is allocated from a global pool, and the block table is updated to point the next logical index to this new physical location. This indirection allows the system to store KV states for different sequences in non-contiguous memory regions, drastically reducing memory fragmentation and increasing GPU memory utilization.

A critical feature of this architecture is its support for **beam search** via a mechanism similar to **copy-on-write**. In beam search, multiple candidate sequences (beams) may share the same prefix. Paged Attention allows these beams to share the same physical KV blocks for the common prefix. When a beam diverges—meaning it generates a different token than its siblings—the system does not immediately copy the entire history. Speculative decoding is an inference optimization technique designed to accelerate the generation process of large language models (LLMs) by leveraging a smaller, faster "draft" model to propose candidate tokens for a larger, more accurate "target" model. This approach fundamentally alters the computational dynamics of autoregressive generation, specifically by reducing the number of sequential forward passes required by the target model.

In standard autoregressive decoding, the target model must generate one token at a time, waiting for the previous token to be processed before moving to the next. This creates a significant bottleneck, as the target model’s forward pass is often the most computationally expensive step. Speculative decoding mitigates this by allowing the draft model to generate a sequence of $k$ candidate tokens in parallel. These candidates are then verified by the target model in a single forward pass. If the target model agrees with the draft’s predictions, all $k$ tokens are accepted, effectively compressing $k$ sequential steps into one. Consequently, the number of target forward passes is reduced by a factor roughly proportional to the acceptance rate, leading to substantial speedups without sacrificing the quality of the output.

The acceptance rate is the critical metric determining the efficiency of this process. It represents the proportion of draft tokens that the target model validates. A high acceptance rate implies that the draft model is a good proxy for the target, maximizing the reduction in target forward passes. Conversely, a low acceptance rate means the target model frequently rejects the draft’s suggestions, forcing it to re-evaluate tokens individually, which diminishes the performance gains.

NVFP4, specifically the E2M1 format, represents a significant leap in extreme low-precision computing, designed primarily to accelerate Large Language Model (LLM) inference by reducing memory bandwidth and compute requirements. The end-to-end workflow begins with **packing**, where 32-bit floating-point weights are converted into 4-bit E2M1 representations. Unlike standard FP8, E2M1 uses 2 bits for the exponent and 1 bit for the mantissa, offering a dynamic range of 0 to 15 but with very coarse granularity. To mitigate the severe precision loss inherent in such a low bit-width, the data is organized into small blocks, typically 16 elements per block.

The core of this quantization scheme lies in the **block scale factors**. For every block of 16 E2M1 values, a single FP8 (or sometimes FP16) scale factor is computed. This scale factor represents the maximum absolute value within that specific block, ensuring that the largest value maps to the maximum representable E2M1 value (15.0). This per-block scaling allows the quantization to adapt locally to the distribution of weights, preserving relative magnitudes within the block even if absolute precision is low. The packed E2M1 data and the corresponding scale factors are stored separately in memory, often in a transposed or interleaved layout to optimize tensor core loading.
